name: Brachioplasty (arm lift)

card.summary: Surgery that removes loose upper-arm skin and fat to give a tighter, more defined arm contour, usually after weight loss or ageing.
card.note: Leaves a scar along the arm; complications include seroma, nerve injury and asymmetry.

quick.overview:
Brachioplasty, or arm lift, reshapes the upper arms and the connecting chest wall by removing sagging skin and, often, fat [1]. It is aimed at loose, hanging arm tissue that has not improved with diet and exercise.

The appearance payoff is a smoother, tighter arm contour that shows better in sleeveless clothing and when physique is on display. Techniques range from liposuction alone to extended skin excision, and newer energy-assisted liposuction methods are studied for people who want to avoid long scars [1][2].
quick.how: A plastic surgeon chooses a technique by how much skin excess there is: liposuction for mostly fat, minimal-incision methods for modest laxity, traditional or extended excision for larger excess, and a fish incision for very large amounts [1]. Scars lie along the underside of the arm and may extend to the chest wall [1].
quick.risks: Wikipedia lists anaesthesia risks, bleeding, infection, blood clots, fluid buildup, skin or tissue death, sensory nerve damage, prolonged swelling, asymmetry, abnormal scarring and possible revision surgery [1]. Scarring is the trade-off patients most often weigh [3].

lead: Brachioplasty, commonly called an arm lift, is surgery to reshape the upper arms and the adjoining chest wall, most often to remove loose skin or fat that has not responded to diet and exercise [1]. The American Society of Plastic Surgeons describes it as reshaping the underside of the upper arm from underarm to elbow, reducing sagging skin, tightening supporting tissue and reducing pockets of fat, for people whose arms sag because of weight fluctuation, ageing or heredity [9].

The appearance payoff is a tighter, smoother and more proportional arm contour that looks better in sleeveless clothing and when the physique is on show, which is why it features in body-contouring plans after major weight loss [7][9][10]. For people building a lean physique through training and dieting, arm skin that does not retract can limit how defined the arm looks, and brachioplasty is the surgical answer described in the plastic surgery literature.

Techniques include liposuction alone, hidden or minimal-incision methods, traditional excision, extended brachioplasty, the fish incision, a non-excisional approach, superficial fascial system suspension and mould-guided incision planning [1]. A 2014 review contrasts the ideal upper arm with sagging deformities and describes the L brachioplasty with liposuction [2], while a randomised trial compared radiofrequency-assisted liposuction and Renuvion helium subdermal coagulation with VASER-assisted liposuction for patients wanting to avoid long scars [3]. ISAPS statistics show global aesthetic procedures reached 34.9 million in 2023 [4].

chain: Excess arm skin and fat removed
Remaining skin is tightened and sutured
angle.text: Removes the sagging 'batwing' tissue so arms look tighter and more proportional, trading it for a scar on the underside of the arm.

infobox: Along underside of arm; shorter or in the axilla with minimal-incision, longer if extended [1][5]

paras: Wikipedia says the term can also describe any surgical arm contouring, and that the operation is often used for loose skin or excess fat in the arms [1]. Common causes of the sagging, sometimes called a 'batwing' contour, are major weight loss, ageing, pregnancy-related change and heredity, according to ASPS [9]. Body-contouring after bariatric surgery targets the arms, buttocks, thighs, abdomen and breasts, and the changes unfold slowly over several years, according to Wikipedia [7]. Plastic surgery reviews treat brachioplasty alongside abdominoplasty, thigh lift and upper-body lift as part of a comprehensive body-lift planning process that begins with medical history, examination and an open discussion with the patient [10][11]. Wikipedia's abdominoplasty entry notes that circumferential trunk procedures are commonly performed after massive weight loss [8].

Wikipedia lists the main approaches with the publications that describe them [1]. CAST liposuction (circumferential para-axillary superficial tumescent liposuction, Gilliland and Lyos, 1997) is a less invasive alternative to deep liposuction that aims to maximise skin retraction. Hidden or minimal-incision brachioplasty (Richards, 2001) suits patients with good skin elasticity and little excess skin; the incision sits in the armpit and combines liposuction, a wide axillary skin excision and dermal suspension. Traditional brachioplasty removes excess skin and leaves a scar along the underside of the upper arm. Extended brachioplasty continues the incision onto the chest wall when loose skin runs that far. The fish incision (Chandawarkar and Lewis, 2006) is marked pre-operatively with measurements for patients with very large soft-tissue excess [1].

Other methods include the non-excisional technique (Ibrahiem, 2020), in which liposuction thins the tissue and only the skin over a marked area is excised with dermal-to-dermal closure to reduce seroma and nerve injury; superficial fascial system suspension (Lockwood, 1995), which anchors the arm flap to the axillary fascia; and mould-guided double S-shaped incisions (de Souza Pinto and colleagues, 2000) for smaller, more symmetrical scars [1]. Non-surgical options combine liposuction with laser, ultrasound or helium plasma; Wikipedia says their long-term results are generally less significant than surgical excision but they leave no visible scar [1]. A 2014 review of minimal-incision brachioplasty reports results equal to the traditional approach in comparable cases, with a low complication rate and high patient satisfaction, and notes that patients with massive weight loss may not meet the criteria [5]. A 2014 review of the L brachioplasty with liposuction describes avoiding post-brachioplasty aesthetic deformity, which it calls difficult to correct [2].

Wikipedia dates the main named techniques from 1995 (superficial fascial system suspension) to 2020 (non-excisional review), with CAST liposuction in 1997 and the fish incision in 2006 [1]. Grokipedia's AI-generated summary attributes the first esthetic arm reduction descriptions to Max Thorek in 1930 and a formal longitudinal brachioplasty to Correa-Iturraspe and Fernandez in the 1950s, and says demand rose from the 1980s as bariatric surgery spread; these dates come from that summary only [16]. The 1990s and 2000s brought liposuction-assisted techniques, and more recently energy-assisted liposuction methods studied for people who want to avoid long scars [1][3].

Traditional brachioplasty leaves a significant scar along the underside of the upper arm, minimal-incision approaches place it in the axilla, and extended procedures run it along the chest wall [1][5]. Scarring is the trade-off patients most often weigh; the authors of a 2022 trial note that many patients refuse surgical treatment for fear of prominent long scars, which motivated testing non-excisional options [3]. Grokipedia states that the operation lasts about two to three hours, is usually outpatient, and is followed by compression garments for several weeks and months of scar maturation [16]. Patients in these reports are typically adults at stable weight and non-smokers [16].

Wikipedia lists anaesthesia risks, bleeding, infection, blood clots, collapsed lung, fluid buildup, skin or tissue death along the wound, sensory nerve damage causing prolonged numbness, prolonged swelling, damage to underlying tissue, asymmetry, abnormal scarring and the need for further surgery [1]. A French review of brachioplasty after major weight loss reports that major complications are rare or not reported in most series, while minor ones such as hypertrophic scarring, wide scars, paraesthesia and wound dehiscence are more common, and that patients sometimes request revision [12]. A 2021 clinical study evaluated the safety of simultaneous circumferential liposuction and brachioplasty in 62 patients [6].

Brachioplasty is part of the body-contouring group: upper body lift combines brachioplasty with upper-back resection and breast reconstruction for massive weight-loss patients, with three resection patterns described, one for males and two for females [11]. Other surgeries discussed alongside it include abdominoplasty, thigh lift and lower body lift [8][10]. Liposuction-assisted brachioplasty has also been studied for breast-cancer-related lymphedema, and a bipolar radiofrequency device has been tested for arm and postpartum fat deposits and skin laxity [13][14]. Case reports describe technical refinements [15].

A randomised trial compared RFAL and Renuvion helium subdermal coagulation with VASER-assisted liposuction for non-excisional arm contouring in patients who wanted to avoid long scars [3]. A 2021 clinical trial of 62 patients (49 women and 13 men) examined the safety of simultaneous circumferential liposuction and brachioplasty [6]. Review articles describe minimal-incision, L-shaped and liposuction-assisted techniques [2][5], and one on complications describes outcomes in post-bariatric patients [12]. ISAPS reports that 34.9 million surgical and non-surgical aesthetic procedures were performed by plastic surgeons worldwide in 2023, a 3.4 percent increase [4].

timeline.event: Superficial fascial system suspension technique described [1].
CAST liposuction described by Gilliland and Lyos [1].
Clinics in Plastic Surgery reviews cover L brachioplasty and limited-scar brachioplasty [2][5].
62-patient study of simultaneous circumferential liposuction and brachioplasty published [6].
Randomised trial of energy-assisted liposuction arm contouring published [3].
ISAPS reports 34.9 million aesthetic procedures worldwide [4].
